sources.news_title: U.S. Food Importing Company Demands Trump for Tariffs on Canadian Products · Global Voices
sources.text:
Empresa importadora de alimentos de Estados Unidos demanda a Trump por aranceles a productos canadienses
La acción judicial busca frenar el cobro de los gravámenes impuestos por Washington a miles de millones de dólares en bienes canadienses, en medio del deterioro de las relaciones comerciales entre ambos países
Washington, Estados Unidos. Uno de los principales importadores de alimentos de Estados Unidos demandó este martes al gobierno de Donald Trump con el fin de anular los aranceles impuestos a ciertos productos canadienses, tras el fracaso de las negociaciones comerciales entre ambos países a principios de este año.
Los aranceles del 50% aplicados por Washington a bienes canadienses por valor de miles de millones de dólares entraron en vigor a finales de agosto, lo que desencadenó una rápida represalia de Ottawa.
Desde entonces, las autoridades estadounidenses han incorporado quesos, embarcaciones a motor y artículos de aluminio a la lista de productos afectados, al tiempo que excluyeron otros clave, como sal para carreteras y cemento.
 
Trump también prohibió la importación de diversos productos alcohólicos y lácteos procedentes de Canadá.
Los derechos del 50% constituyeron “el último intento del gobierno de Trump de ejercer, mediante una norma que nunca fue diseñada para ese fin, el poder arancelario que la Constitución asigna al Congreso”, argumenta la demanda presentada por Gellert Global Group.
Para imponer los gravámenes a Canadá, Trump recurrió a una disposición legal poco conocida, la Sección 338 de la Ley Arancelaria de 1930.
Pero la empresa pidió al Tribunal de Comercio Internacional de Estados Unidos que declare los aranceles “ilegales” y suspenda su aplicación y cobro.
Disputa entre Canadá y Estados Unidos
Canadá es uno de los principales socios comerciales de Estados Unidos.
Sin embargo, desde que volvió a la presidencia en enero de 2025, Trump ha impuesto amplios aranceles tanto a aliados como a competidores de Estados Unidos, y también ha gravado sectores que van desde el acero hasta la industria automotriz.
Sin embargo, los gravámenes dirigidos a sectores concretos siguen vigentes.
Aunque más tarde Trump recurrió a otros mecanismos legales para reconstruir su política arancelaria, el fallo del máximo tribunal limitó de forma significativa su capacidad para imponer rápidamente nuevas tarifas a sus socios.
Los aranceles cruzados entre Estados Unidos y Canadá afectan a un volumen relativamente pequeño de su comercio bilateral.
Pero los vínculos entre los vecinos norteamericanos se han deteriorado en los últimos tiempos.
Trump ha aludido numerosas veces a Canadá como el posible estado número 51 de Estados Unidos y ha calificado al primer ministro canadiense Mark Carney de “gobernador”.
En agosto, Trump firmó un decreto para renombrar el lago Ontario, en la frontera con Canadá, como “Lago América”.
La medida provocó indignación en Canadá en medio de una ola más amplia de patriotismo desencadenada por la hostilidad del líder estadounidense.

sources.news_title: Food importer files lawsuit to block Trump's Canada tariffs
Lawsuit Challenges Trump's Tariffs on Canadian Goods
sources.text:
A U.S. food importer has filed a lawsuit in the United States Court of International Trade challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs targeting Canada.
The lawsuit, filed Tuesday by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of Gellert Global Group in the New York-based court, argued Trump's use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president.
"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht said in a news release.
Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August.
The same statute was used the following month to ban the import of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.
The White House has said Section 338 empowers the president to impose tariffs when a country puts U.S. exporters at a disadvantage relative to exporters in other countries — even though the law has never been used for that purpose.
U.S. officials have said the latest duties are a response to provincial bans on U.S. liquor, Canada's supply managed dairy system and quotas on certain U.S. vehicles.
Tuesday's lawsuit said the Canadian policies don't justify the sweeping tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.
It notes two of the measures — auto quotas and liquor bans — were actually a response to Trump's own tariff measures. The lawsuit also said Canada's dairy supply management involves policies agreed to under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as CUSMA, which was negotiated during the first Trump administration.
The White House has not yet responded to a request for comment.
Thomas Gellert, co-chief executive officer of Gellert Global Group, said the company has "spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry."
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," Gellert said in the news release.
The case raises concerns beyond Canada, the news release said. If the duties remain unchecked, any president could use Section 338 to impose tariffs and trade restrictions without meaningful congressional control.
The Liberty Justice Center was previously involved in the legal challenge against Trump's use of the International Economic Emergency Powers Act of 1977 for the so-called "Liberation Day" and fentanyl-related tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.
In February, America's top court concluded it was not legal for Trump to use the statute, known as IEEPA, because the U.S. Constitution very clearly gives Congress power over taxes and tariffs.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

sources.news_title: US food importer sues Trump over 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods
sources.text:
US food importer sues Trump over 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods
The lawsuit argues Trump bypassed Congress and misused a century-old law to impose sweeping tariffs on Canadian imports.
A US food importer is suing US President Donald Trump over his 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods, arguing he lacks the legal authority to impose sweeping tariffs without congressional approval.
Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based company that imports Canadian cheese, filed the lawsuit on Tuesday in the US Court of International Trade in New York.
The company says the tariffs are driving up its costs and disrupting its relationships with suppliers on both sides of the border. Between September 16 and October 11, Gellert had paid more than $520,000 in duties, according to the complaint.
“Gellert Global Group has spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry,” said Thomas Gellert, the company’s co-chief executive officer, in a press release. “These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain.”
The lawsuit challenges Trump’s decision to use a Depression-era law to impose tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products, including dairy products, furniture, clothing and wine.
Trump first imposed the 50 percent tariffs over the summer, accusing Canada of discriminating against American-made cars, alcohol and dairy products. He expanded the measures in September, adding more products in response to Canadian retaliatory tariffs.
The lawsuit argues that the law doesn’t apply to the Canadian policies the Trump administration says are discriminatory, since two of them “arose in response to the president’s own tariffs, while the third involves Canadian dairy policy governed by the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA)”.
It also questions why Canadian cheese is being taxed over disputes involving alcohol and cars.
“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” said Sara Albrecht, chairman and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center, a nonprofit legal organisation that filed the suit on Gellert’s behalf.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, according to the Reuters news agency.
At the centre of the case is Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on imports from countries found to discriminate against American businesses.
The provision had never been used until Trump invoked it this year.
The lawsuit argues that newer laws passed by Congress since then, such as Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, require investigations, public comment and other safeguards that Gellert says the Trump administration has bypassed, and that these override Section 338.
“The administration cannot skip those protections by reaching for a 1930 statute that no president had ever used to impose a tariff,” said Jeffrey Schwab, the Liberty Justice Center’s senior counsel and director of litigation.
In addition, the lawsuit says that even if Trump is allowed to use the older law, he hasn’t met its requirements, including waiting 30 days before tariffs can be collected on new products added to the list.
The administration only waited seven days to start collecting tariffs on cheese in September, according to the lawsuit.
Gellert is asking the court to declare the tariffs illegal, stop them from being collected, and order refunds with interest for importers who have been impacted.
The lawsuit marks the fourth major legal challenge to Trump’s tariffs.
In February, the US Supreme Court struck down most of the tariffs he imposed in 2025, and a trade court later ruled against a temporary 10 percent global tariff. A separate challenge to tariffs imposed over alleged forced labour in international trade is still pending.

sources.news_title: Cheese Importer Sues Trump Over 50% Canada Tariffs
sources.text:
CNBC reports:
A new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump’s invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff.
“Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy” that has been “impliedly repealed” by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says. The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.

sources.news_title: New Jersey food importer files lawsuit challenging Trump’s 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A New Jersey food importer filed a lawsuit Tuesday challenging President Donald Trump’s power to invoke a Depression-era law to levy a 50% tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
The Gellert Global Group, a third-generation family business that imports Canadian cheese, took its case to the U.S. Court of International Trade, a specialized court in New York.
In August, Trump reached back to Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose the tariffs on Canada, prompting dollar-for-dollar retaliation from Ottawa and straining already-tense relations between the neighbors and longtime allies. The president last month escalated the conflict by announcing an outright ban on nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian products, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.
The president’s Section 338 tariff authority had never been used in a trade dispute, let alone tested in court.
“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” said Sara Albrecht, chair of the Liberty Justice Center, a libertarian advocacy group that is representing the Gellert firm and which successfully challenged previous Trump tariffs before the Supreme Court earlier this year.
The White House said the administration would vigorously defend Trump’s tariffs on Canadian imports and considers Section 338 appropriate to counter what the administration considers Canadian discrimination against American dairy, alcohol and auto exports.
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has sought to build a wall of protective tariffs — import taxes — around the U.S. economy. The centerpiece of the policy originally was his use of a 1977 law to declare America’s longstanding trade deficits a national emergency, justifying double-digit tariffs on almost every country. But the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, and the Trump administration was forced to refund billions of dollars to the importers that paid them.
Trump has since looked for other legal authority to tax imports. In July, for example, he hit dozens of U.S. trading partners with tariffs of 10% to 12.5%, charging that they had not done enough to crack down on imports produced by forced labor. Those tariffs are also being challenged in court.
Then he invoked Section 338 to sanction Canada for allegedly discriminating against U.S. dairy, auto and alcoholic beverages.
As Section 338 sat on the books unused for decades, Congress passed new trade laws. Some of them ceded to the president tariff power, which the Constitution originally granted to Congress. But the new laws also limited the president’s authority to certain circumstances — including dealing with national security threats and foreign currency crises — and required the government to carry out investigations and meet other procedural requirements beforehand.
The Liberty Justice Center argues that the newer trade legislation superseded the president’s Section 338 tariff authority and rendered it obsolete.

Trump faces lawsuit over tariffs on Canada
sources.text:
The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August, BBC reported.
***
The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.
The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused “immediate harm to American businesses”.
The White House has been contacted for comment.
Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.
Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.
“These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain,” he said on Tuesday.
The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration’s use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.
That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch “to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises”.
The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House’s reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs “dollar for dollar” after Trump imposed them for what he called “unequal treatment” of US cars, dairy and alcohol.
It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.
Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.
“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” she said.
